recommendations.text: To take measures to increase the awareness of veterinarians both at slaughterhouses and in the field to ensure that all bovines displaying behavioural or neurological signs, where the disease can not be ruled out on the basis of response to treatment or following laboratory examination, are notified to the Competent Authorities. With regard to the feed ban:
To review the sampling method used to ensure compliance with Commission Directive 76/371/EEC.
To use a risk based targeted approach in the sampling programme in accordance with the principles laid down in Council Directive 95/53/EC.
To issue clear procedures for cases where positive samples are detected ensuring that actions to be taken are rapid and effective. With regard to SRM:
To ensure that SRM is properly stained at slaughterhouses.
To consider using clearly identifiable dedicated containers for the collection and transport of SRM.
To ensure reconciliation of SRM throughout the whole chain from removal to destruction or storage.
To ensure that veterinary certification accompanying consignments of SRM is in compliance with Council Directive 96/93/EC.
To fully control the flow of SRM consignments sent to Denmark, and to ensure full compliance with Commission Decision 97/735/EC.

To find a solution to increase the rendering capacity for SRM and to ensure safe disposal of this material. 27 9. ADDENDUM TO MISSION REPORT 3236/2001 Competent Authority response to the recommendations in the report The Swedish authorities stated in their comments that: 1. Additional training for veterinarians started in spring 2001. The purpose of the training is to increase BSE awareness among Sweden's practising veterinarians and veterinary inspectors. 2. Sweden is gradually progressing towards full compliance with Directive 96/371/EEC concerning testing for MBM in feedingstuffs. 3. Sweden now applies the zero tolerance principle as regards the action limit in case of detection of MBM in feedingstuff. If it is established that cattle received feed containing traces of MBM, they will be included in the monitoring programme now in force. 4. Veterinary inspectors have been asked to ensure tight supervision of SRM staining. 5. Clear marking of containers used for SRM, from slaughterhouses to rendering plant, has been introduced. 6. Reconciliation procedures for SRM have been introduced. Indicative figures on the weight of SRM are now available in slaughterhouses and rendering plants. These routines are also checked in conjunction with slaughterhouse surveillance reports. 7. Under the agreement with the Danish authorities the requirement for veterinary certification has been abolished, and SRM consignments are now accompanied by a commercial document. 8. SRM containers sent to Denmark are now sealed and the seal number is put on the commercial document. An ANIMO message is now sent from Denmark to Sweden to confirm the arrival of consignments. 9. recommendations.text: To actively monitor the BSE surveillance system (including cross-checks) in order to ensure that all eligible fallen stock are sampled. With regard to TSE controls in ovine and caprine animals (EC Reg. 999/2001):

To set up guidelines for the official controls on identification and registration in small ruminants and a system to record these controls and their results in order to demonstrate that the relevant requirements are enforced.
To evaluate the sampling programme periodically in order to ensure that over- or under-representation, for example of any breed or production type of animals, does not occur. (28) See footnote 12. 28

To improve the overall efficacy of the monitoring programme in fallen stock by: · Ensuring the delivery by the farmers of all fallen stock for rendering. · Establishing official controls of the eligibility of the fallen stock to be sampled at the rendering plant. With regard to the feed ban:
To amend the sampling method used for sampling of feed in order to ensure that all parts of Commission Directive 76/371 are complied with.

To include criteria as type of feed produced, sourcing of raw materials, number and structure of production lines, previous testing and inspection results in the targeting of samples when setting up the sampling programme.
To issue official instructions in order to include cattle from farms that have received feed contaminated with MBM in the monitoring programme.
To ensure the implementation of procedures for the tracing and withdrawal of contaminated feed in case of detection of MBM.

To implement a control system of the transport of feed from the feedmills to the farms in order to ensure that ruminant feed is not cross-contaminated with monogastric feed containing fishmeal during transport.
To ensure that retailers selling fishmeal are officially authorised. With regard to SRM:

To include the SRM rendering plants in the official controls regarding channelling/reconciliation of SRM in order to verify that all plants producing SRM deliver expected amounts to these rendering plants.
To ensure that consignments of SRM destined to Denmark are accompanied by a health certificate.
To consider implementing a system of audits from the central level in order to ensure a sufficient level of control in the various municipalities.

To ensure that the companies' own checks programmes include elements of checks/controls (including documentation from these) in order to make it possible for the official services to verify the efficacy of these programmes. 29 ADDENDUM TO MISSIOIN REPORT 8567/2002 Competent Authority response to the recommendations in the report The Swedish authorities announced in their written comments of 19 August 2002 that they had taken the following actions in relation to the recommendations: · Monitoring of BSE surveillance will be improved once the new occurrence codes for the notification to the database are used everywhere. · Inspections for the official controls on the identification and registration in small ruminants are carried out by the County authorities in conjunction with inspections relating to ewe subsidies. · Discussions are underway within the BSE reference group how to ensure that no breed or production type is over- or under represented. recommendations.text: During official controls, to ensure that food business operators comply with the requirements of Article 8 of Regulation (EC) No 1169/2011 as well as Article 18 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002, in regard to traceability, including qualitative and quantitative aspects.

citations.text: In one establishment, the FBO archived incoming and outgoing documentation without any additional registration regarding the different origins, quantities of raw materials received and processed and quantities of final products. A batch number was created per day of production. The quantities of the pigs' heads received and the approval number of the establishment that had delivered the meat were not recorded. No specific batch number was created when organic cutting production was carried out. The dates of production of organic meat were not recorded. No information concerning the quantities of meat of different batches delivered to the clients was available. As a consequence the establishments could not carry out any quantitative exercise or any reconciliation. No documented traceability system was in place to allow a recall to be adequately carried out.

Another establishment was directly importing Halal meat from Third Countries. The establishment did not have the Common Veterinary Entry Documents available relating to the consignments evaluated by the FVO audit team. Halal meat was also coming from Member States. The FBO had decided to implement, on a voluntary basis, the Swedish requirement that animals should be stunned before being Halal slaughtered for any meat imported or traded. This requirement could not be documented for deliveries coming from Member States and Third Countries. The traceability system was based on the recording of the date of slaughter at slaughterhouse level, but the FBO could not provide data concerning the quantities of meat present in the establishment for each of the slaughter dates. The storage was made by article number. As a consequence, different slaughter dates were mixed on the same pallet and the owner had no documented system in place for retrieving the meat belonging to different incoming consignments. Neither quantitative traceability nor reconciliation could be carried out by the FVO audit team.

In a third establishment, delivery notes accompanying the incoming deliveries were archived in a binder. The quantities of meat arriving at the establishment were not documented in another way. The traceability system was based on the packing date which was used as batch number. Nevertheless, the internal traceability could not be demonstrated. The quantities used at production level were not registered. The 5 labelling of the bovine meat in consumer packs was not in line with Regulation (EC) No 1760/2000, although the information to allow for a correct labelling was available.

A fourth establishment had a system in place foreseeing the manual recording of the quantities of ingredients received and the references/approval number of the slaughterhouses having produced the incoming meat. However this did not provide the reference of the establishment directly delivering the meat. A lot number specific to the establishment visited was attributed for each entering consignment based on the approval number of the slaughterhouse having produced the meat. A batch number was created for each new production. No recording of the final production quantities was carried out except when the FBO carried out internal reconciliation exercises. The exact quantities of each production batch for the goods delivered to the clients were not recorded.

In a fifth establishment, a batch number was automatically generated for each pallet or group of pallets belonging to the same purchase order and arriving on the same day. All the batch numbers were recorded in the business system of the company. Once identified and registered, each pallet could be allocated to the production departments where a new batch number was created for any given production carried out. This new batch number was created using the week, the day within the week and an increasing chronological number during the week. Reworks were taken into consideration in the traceability system, but not the timing for these reworks to be processed. At present, there is no system in place for carrying out reconciliation exercises. No system was in place for detecting anomalies between the quantities of meat in store and the quantities of meat used for the production. Also no documented evidence existed linking the production of the batch to the packing date. The batch number was not present on the goods sold to the consumers, but only on the trays sold to the supermarket.

In a sixth establishment, the FBO put a traceability system in place including the bar coding of the incoming raw material and outgoing meat products. All consignments of ingredients (e.g. meat, offal, spices) entering the establishment were checked and attributed a bar code. A batch number was created for the production of a given product on any given day. This batch could include one or more recipes. The preparation of each recipe included the scanning of the bar code of all ingredients used and it was explained that the system could automatically deduct the quantities of ingredient picked up from the stock. Nevertheless there was no physical validation of the real weight used for each ingredient used. On the day of the FVO visit, the system was also not able to provide the quantities of meat products produced for each batch, making any reconciliation impossible between the data relating to the initial ingredients and the final products. The FBO explained that no reconciliation system for the final products was in place. Anomalies were detected between the percentage of meat physically present in the recipe of a given meat product and the percentage of meat mentioned on the label.

A seventh establishment had a sophisticated traceability system in place: the batch numbers allocated were based on the date of production of the products, the article 6 number and the internal number of the establishment within the group of companies they belong to. The batch number was present on the trays sent to supermarket but not on the consumer packs. A new batch number was created for any movement of raw material, ingredients, half products or products. Nevertheless, in one of the two cases evaluated by the FVO audit team the data recorded in the company system did not match what the company claimed as being the physical reality, e.g. a production of the 18/03/2015 was recorded as being produced on the 19/03/2015, making the traceability exercise impossible. A consignment note of organic livers received in this establishment mentioned an article number which, after verification by the NFA, proved to be the same for organic and non-organic livers. The FBO gave a commitment to create a specific article number for organic livers.

The only cold store visited had a robust system in place based on the bar coding of any single entering pallet of meat. This bar code is scanned and registered in the system as well as the physical location of any bar coded pallet. As soon as an order is received for exiting goods, the system designates the palettes to be extracted from the cold store using the first in first out principle. The exiting goods are scanned allowing the cold store to have an ongoing permanent state of play of all goods stored. The exercises carried out by the FVO team revealed only one minor deficiency relating to one tray of meat.

In all the establishments visited, the FBOs stated that a traceability system was in place. However, the evaluation of these systems revealed a less positive picture concerning traceability in general and quantitative traceability in particular. In one cold store a robust system was in place. Two establishments were making good progress towards implementing a good system but the others still had significant progress to make. Two establishments had yet to start work on implementing a traceability system.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the official controls are carried out in an effective way so as to achieve food business operators' compliance with general and specific hygiene requirements as required by Articles 3 and 4 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, in particular ensuring that sufficient resources and time are allocated to allow in-depth checks that cover all control requirements over a shorter span.

citations.text: The audit team was informed that in order to ensure that controls are carried out adequately, the following measures were put in place: On a regular basis, in each region a verification is undertaken to check that, at team level, planned controls are being carried out, non-compliances are followed-up within deadlines set, and that control reports are sent to FBOs within 14 days. Starting from 2018 all CAs (CABs, regional NFA and MCAs) must report to the central NAF office on the controls performed, which establishments have been controlled, the legislative scope of the controls, and on the non-compliances found. The intention is to collect better data in order to support determining the focus of controls for the following year. In order to ensure consistency, senior officials at regional level review reports and documented enforcement actions. In addition, on-site supervisory visits are carried out either by these senior staff, alone or jointly with the officials that routinely carry out controls. Joint visits between different OVs also take place. A minimum of two joint official controls per year are required to be carried out by each local CA carrying out visits on the spot. In some cases, as a result of these joint visits where one OV observes other OV's control performance, recommendations for improvements of the controls were made . Nonetheless, these supervisory activities did not identify certain occasions where official controls failed to identify certain non-compliances(see Sections 5.3.3 and 5.3.4) An overall quality management system will be developed during 2018.

The system in place also includes reporting of and supervision over the activities carried out by official staff with the objective of verifying the implementation of official controls and the performance of the OV of the official controls. However, this system was not fully effective in detecting certain gaps in the controls, and therefore not capable of prompting appropriate corrective action in these instances.

The control staff organise the work, including how often to go on-the-spot, depending on the number of hours assigned to each establishment. The frequency of controls is related to the number of allocated hours (e.g. a registered cold store receives one hour per year which results in visits on the spot every few years when sufficient hours have accumulated, while a stand-alone meat establishment which receives more hours, may receive several control visits per year). These hours include preparation for the control, carrying out the on-site control and drafting the report (one third of the allocated time for each of these activities), which are then charged directly to the FBO concerned. 5

The hours allocated to perform certain controls might not support an in-depth evaluation in all situations. For example, a large meat products establishment with several production lines received 15 hours/year for controls, of which five hours occur on the spot; for one the biggest cutting plants, also producing meat preparations and minced meat, 39 hours for controls per year had been allocated; while for a medium sized meat preparations and meat product establishment ­ 20 hours had been assigned for the year.

All establishments visited had established HACCP-based systems. Official controls include as part of the routine controls and/or during audits the verification of these systems and the evidence available showed that the controls had been carried out as described and, in general, did identify very few shortcomings. The official controls also covered checks on pre-requisite programmes such as potable water, cleaning, disinfection and pest control.

Official controls are in general organised in line with EU requirements, their frequency 15 is risk-based and they follow specific documented procedures including those related to enforcement. However, the lack of resources, the time limitations to perform in-depth checks, the lack of details in the reports and the delegation of certain tasks to the FBOs without effective oversight, affects the overall efficiency of the official controls.
While the system of official controls includes checks on FCI and animal identification, these are not fully reliable and are not sufficient to guarantee that any non-compliances are detected.
CAs follow-up on identified non-compliances, but the measures taken did not address the cause in some cases.

citations.text: For each of the areas of controls assessed, instruction and guidance for controls had been issued by the NFA and made available by NFA both on their website in the "Kontrollportalen", which is available to all control authorities, as well as in "Kontrollwiki" which is also available to FBOs and consumers. For the areas assessed, the control staff is made aware of the legislation relevant to the area of control, and suggestions for questions to the FBOs are prepared.

National instructions on the identification of animals for slaughter (2015-09-04/BMODA) lay down the responsibilities of animal keepers, transporters, FBOs and the OVs. However, the verification of the identification of animals is done by the FBO after slaughter and not on the live animals, which is not in line with EU requirements or with point 5, third paragraph, of this instruction. Implementation of controls and resources

In the majority of the cases, official controls had been carried out according to the plan, with an exception for the region Central-North which continues to encounter difficulties with staff recruitment despite efforts to improve manpower levels. In this region, and depending on the time of year, a shortfall of up to 10 % in required numbers was noted for 2017;there is a need to employ nine additional staff in 2018. One additional staff member was recruited in 2018. As a result of staff shortage, not all the planned controls can or have been done. e.g. in one large establishment packing products for consumers, only 40% of the attributed and planned hours for 2017 for official controls (20.5 hours of controls instead of 47 hours) had been used. This establishment was already under reduced frequency of controls due to CA staff shortages.

In the northern part of the country, the CAs faces challenges for the implementation of the controls due to the great distances between establishments, the concentration of the slaughter in certain times of the year and the lack of internet connection (all CA documents are in electronic format).

In the same region, it is planned that staff working in slaughterhouses carry out other controls in the months of the year with low slaughter activity. A system is in place to 7 appoint OVs on a temporary basis for the times of the year with higher volumes. These veterinarians, already employed by the SBA, are appointed by the NFA on a yearly or once every two years basis. For new temporary recruits a permanently employed OV from NFA provides induction training, all the required information and on-the-job training related to OV's specific duties. It is only when the latter is satisfied that the temporary OV is allowed to carry out his assigned official tasks independently. 5.3.2 Reporting of official control results

Starting from 2018 a new report template is in use in several MCAs, including Gothenburg and Stockholm. The use of the new template by all NFA staff is delayed pending the organisation of training courses on how to write the reports. The template provides for the inclusion of all items checked during the controls - the previous system reported only on identified non-compliances- and includes details on the FBO's corrective actions in response to non-compliances from previous controls.

audits.title: Import controls for plant health

recommendations.text: Ensure that meticulous inspections are carried out on at least each lot declared, under the customs formalities, to consist of, or to contain, plants or plant products referred to in Article 13(1), (2) or (3) of Directive 2000/29/EC, in line with Article 13a(1)(a)(ii) of the same Directive. Ensure that these inspections are carried out on the entirety of the lot, or a representative sample, in line with Article 13a(1)(b)(ii) and (iii) of the same Directive.

citations.text: The instructions on sampling stipulate that the sample taken from 'mixed consignments' should be constituted of units from the different regulated commodities within the consignment, based on an ad hoc risk assessment by the inspector, to make up the minimum sample of 200 units. The sample unit is defined as the 'minimum single part of the commodity', e.g. a single cut flower stem, a stem of leafy vegetables, an individual piece of fruit or vegetable, or an individual plant intended for planting. The audit team noted from inspection data supplied by the SBA, that a significant proportion of consignments imported into Sweden are 'mixed', including around 50 consignments per year of aquarium plants of mixed genera from Southeast Asia.

The audit team observed inspections of mixed consignments containing fruits and vegetables from Uganda and Thailand at Arlanda airport and noted that the work instructions were followed, and that sampling for visual checks was based on the consignment and not on the individual, constituent lots. The number of units of each regulated article taken to form the sample varied significantly (see section 5.4.4 below). Inspections are not therefore carried out on the entirety or a representative sample of at least each lot declared to consist of, or to contain, plants or plant products referred to in Article 13(1), (2) or (3) of Directive 2000/29/EC. This is not in line with Article 13a(1)(a)(ii) or 13a(1)(b)(ii) or (iii) of the same Directive.

However, in line with the work instructions, inspections of mixed consignments are not carried out on a representative sample of each constituent lot. These checks do not therefore provide an appropriate level of confidence or probability of detecting any harmful organisms that may be present.

The audit team noted that, with respect to sampling: Inspectors selected the sample for inspection themselves and were free from interference from third parties; The size of samples taken for inspection was in line with the work instructions (see section 5.1.4 above); At Frihamnen Stockholm, the inspector could only access the rearmost pallets of the container to collect a sample for visual checks, and so it could not be ensured that the samples was representative of the consignment, as required by Article 13a(1)(b)(iii) of Directive 2000/29/EC; At the other inspection posts visited, inspectors had access to the entire consignment and samples were collected from a range of packages selected at random from different areas within the consignment. In the case of homogenous consignments, the sample could therefore be considered representative of the consignment, as required by Article 13a(1)(b)(iii) of Directive 2000/29/EC; The audit team observed three inspections of mixed consignments. For one of these consignments, the PCU inspectors explained that they had selected one box of each regulated commodity, from which they would inspect 200 units in total. In practice, the sample was constituted as follows (the figures are approximate as the number of units varied slightly between packages): six fruits of bitter melon (Momordica charantia) from a total of 20 fruit; 50 stems of basil (Ocimum basilicum) from a total of 4 500 stems; 40 fruits of aubergine (Solanum melongena) from a total of 400 fruit; 20 fruits of mango (Mangifera indica) from a total of 280 fruit; 50 stems of celery (Apium graveolens) from a total of 1 000 stems; and more than 200 fruits of chillies (Capsicum frutescens) ­ 2.5 kilograms from a total of 34.5 kilograms. In some cases, these sample sizes provide a confidence level significantly below 80% of detecting even a 5% level of infestation according to ISPM 31, and this reduced level of confidence was not justified based on risk.

Other than at Frihamnen Stockholm, import inspections in Sweden are carried out meticulously, and other than mixed consignments, the samples taken for inspection can be considered representative, in line with EU legislation.

recommendations.text: Ensure that any exemptions from the application of Article 13(1) of Directive 2000/29/EC, established for plants and plant products, apply only to small quantities provided that there is no risk of harmful organisms spreading in the Community, in line with Article 13b(3) of the same Directive.

citations.text: Sweden has established an exemption from the requirement for a phytosanitary certificate for certain imports from European third countries only, under Section 17 of the Plant Health Ordinance. The exemption is detailed on the SBA's8 website. The scope of the exemption is as follows: Passengers travelling from European third countries (including the Canary Islands) may import 2 kilograms of plants and plant products in their hand luggage, without a phytosanitary certificate. Private persons moving home, from European third countries (including the Canary Islands) may import any quantity of plants and plant products without a phytosanitary certificate. Neither of these exemptions applies to potatoes, citrus plants, or endangered species.

The exemption for passengers' luggage, concerns only small quantities and is in line with Article 13(3)(b) of Directive 2000/29/EC. However, the exemption for persons moving home, which the SBA stated is intended to reduce the administrative burden of such relocations, is not limited and does not therefore apply only to small quantities, which is not in line with the same article.
However, the unlimited exemption for most plants and plant products imported into Sweden from European third countries by individuals moving home, presents an unmitigated phytosanitary risk.

responses.response: The Swedish government has initiated the revision of the plant ordinance (2006:817) in the context of the new EU regulations 2016/2031 and 2017/625. During this process the ption for individuals moving home from a European third country will be removed.

citations.text: During their visit to the inspection post at Frihamnen Stockholm, where there are regular imports of flower bulbs and citrus fruits from Egypt (intended for juicing), the audit team noted that: There were no inspection facilities, including suitable areas for inspection, adequate lighting, or inspection tables. In the case of homogenous consignments, the sample could therefore be considered representative of the consignment, as required by Article 13a(1)(b)(iii) of Directive 2000/29/EC; The audit team observed three inspections of mixed consignments. For one of these consignments, the PCU inspectors explained that they had selected one box of each regulated commodity, from which they would inspect 200 units in total. In practice, the sample was constituted as follows (the figures are approximate as the number of units varied slightly between packages): six fruits of bitter melon (Momordica charantia) from a total of 20 fruit; 50 stems of basil (Ocimum basilicum) from a total of 4 500 stems; 40 fruits of aubergine (Solanum melongena) from a total of 400 fruit; 20 fruits of mango (Mangifera indica) from a total of 280 fruit; 50 stems of celery (Apium graveolens) from a total of 1 000 stems; and more than 200 fruits of chillies (Capsicum frutescens) ­ 2.5 kilograms from a total of 34.5 kilograms. In some cases, these sample sizes provide a confidence level significantly below 80% of detecting even a 5% level of infestation according to ISPM 31, and this reduced level of confidence was not justified based on risk.

The audit team noted that, with respect to the implementation of the checks: Inspectors had a good knowledge of the different harmful organisms which the commodities they were inspecting were most likely to host; At Frihamnen Stockholm, due to the lack of facilities enabling access to consignments, the inspector selected individual fruit for visual checks one-by-one, returning the fruit each time to the bulk bin. It could not therefore be ensured that the same unit was not inspected more than once. The checks could not therefore be considered meticulous, which is not in line with Article 13a(1)(a) of Directive 2000/29/EC; Other than at Frihamnen Stockholm, the checks observed by the audit team included a thorough visual examination of the entire sample and units which 17 exhibited any signs or symptoms of the presence of harmful organisms were studied carefully using a stereo microscope, and/or destructively sampled. The checks were considered by the audit team to be meticulous, in line with Article 13a(1)(a) of Directive 2000/29/EC.

The lack of inspection facilities at Frihamnen Stockholm means that it is not possible for inspectors to carry out meticulous inspections of representative samples of imported consignments. These checks cannot therefore be considered reliable.

citations.text: The Board of Agriculture monitors whether the county administrative boards achieve these operational objectives. As a result of this monitoring, the Board of Agriculture stated that all counties now use the risk classification model. The county visited by the audit team used the risk classification model but pointed out several problems with the data provided and therefore they used their own local knowledge to some degree when selecting farms for controls. The Board of Agriculture have not evaluated how the risk classification model performs in practice and how effective it is in identifying risk.

The Swedish Board of Agriculture has developed a quality assurance system in 2010 called Animal Welfare declaration (Djurskyddsdeklaration). Herd veterinarians in Sweden working in pig farms who can allow pig farmers the right to administer certain medicines, conditional on a visit every five weeks from their private veterinarian where this quality assurance system is used at farm level. These veterinarians have received training and make a declaration after every visit on compliance with certain animal welfare criteria. The Farm and animal health organisation (Gård & Djurhälsan) employs many such veterinarians. The farmer has to provide an action plan to address any deficiencies, and if the deficiencies persist then the veterinarian must notify the county administrative board. No cases were notified to the county visited. The county administrative board agreed that this was a potentially valuable source of information for risk based planning of official controls. However this lack of notifications presented a very different picture of the level of compliance compared to the result of official controls.

Both the Ministry and the Board of Agriculture work on the premise that the higher level objectives will be met if they ensure compliance with the legislation. The Multi-Annual National Control Plan also contains operational objectives which are specific and measurable and which the Board of Agriculture use to measure the performance of the county administrative boards. This has been successful in ensuring that the 21 county administrative boards work in a more consistent way; however, the evaluation has been more on doing things in the correct manner, rather than evaluating if the control system leads to doing the correct things. So although all counties now use the risk classification model, the objective for "a good risk based" control has not been measured as the Board of Agriculture has not reviewed or evaluated the effectiveness or efficiency of the implementation of the risk classification model.

recommendations.text: To ensure that instances of raw milk containing residues of antibiotics detected by food business operators are reported without delay, and that enforcement actions are taken in line with Article 138.1 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and Article 50 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627 and in a timely fashion, to ensure that raw milk containing antibiotic residues is not entering the food chain.

citations.text: Cases of non-compliances in relation to raw milk quality (PC, SCC or antibiotic residues/inhibitory substances) notified monthly by dairy establishments are usually followed up during the next planned inspection, and not immediately after the county veterinarians receive the reports from the CAB unit dealing with controls over the primary sector. This practice hampers the CAs efforts to take action to determine the origin and extent of the non-compliance in line with Article 138.1 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The immediate measures are left to the dairy establishments and comprise an immediate stop of further deliveries in case of antibiotic residues. Milk payment reduction is also used by 13 the dairy establishments. The situation varied between the CABs reviewed. The CAB Västra Götaland has established a routine where the county official veterinarian carries out an unplanned check on-site as soon as work planning allows. In relation to PC and SCC exceeding values, a risk assessment is made. If there is a sale of small quantities of raw milk from the farm, an unplanned check is carried out on the farm as soon as work planning allows. Otherwise, the plant will be placed on a priority list for targeted planned controls in the coming control year. The CAB of Västernorrland stated that usually there would be no follow-up inspection. Thus, positive cases for residues of inhibitory substances in raw milk are, in general, not timely followed up at holding level as part of official controls. Conclusions on controls over milk and colostrum production holdings

The reporting by FBO to CABs of non-compliances concerning the quality of raw milk (PC and/or SCC), and detection of residues of antibiotics in raw milk, on a monthly basis only, hinders effective follow-up, which is further impacted by systemic delays at the level of the CAB. Equally, positive findings for residues of antibiotics/inhibitory substances are, in general, not timely followed up with official controls at holding level. This is not in line with Article 138.1 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and Article 50.2 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627.

Although the presence of antibiotic residues was deemed a critical control point (CCP) in the HACCP plan of the third larger dairy plant visited by the audit team, the milk trucks were only tested once weekly randomly for inhibitory substances/antibiotic residues, and the test result of the raw milk silo was used to decide if the milk was fit for human consumption. This practice was in line with the branch guidelines. In addition, the use by FBOs of rapid tests that detect beta-lactams and tetracyclines only, implies that other possible antibiotic residues in raw milk would remain undetected.

The FBOs' systems in place in relation to SCC and PC in raw co milk is generally implemented in line with the requirements with Section IX of Annex III, Regulation (EC) No 853/2004, whereas the verification and enforcement action by the CAs after notification of non-compliances in relation to these parameters and/or after detecting antibiotic residues in raw milk is not in line with Article 138.1 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and Article 50.2 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627 as it is done with a delay.

recommendations.text: To design and implement surveillance for HPAI in wild birds in a way that is appropriate and proportionate to its objectives, to act as an early warning system for the possible incursion of the disease in the Swedish territory. Articles 26(2) and (4), and 27 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429. Articles 3(1)(a) and (b)(i), 4(1)(b)(i), and 10(2) of, and Annex II to Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/689. , and

citations.text: The monitoring of HPAI in wild birds is based on reporting and sampling of fallen, or sick and killed animals. Prior to the epizootics, the SVA and the SBA reminded the public and ornithologists of the importance to report those findings to enhance 6 surveillance for HPAI in wild birds. Reports of observed morbidity and mortality in wild birds are analysed on a daily basis and a subset of the birds are submitted to SVA for analysis. As a result, between 400 and 500 wild birds are surveyed annually. However, neither the risk assessments of the SVA, nor the SBA, identified the relevance of adapting and strengthening that surveillance in certain areas of the country in close vicinity to some of the HPAI outbreaks confirmed, where there was a significant presence of species of wild waterfowl that do not regularly show obvious clinical signs of HPAI or increased mortality (e.g. wild geese). This could have provided them with additional epidemiological evidence to reinforce disease preventive activities in the area and to confirm their hypotheses on the local introduction of the HPAI virus from these wild birds into domestic poultry (i.e., carrying out phylogenetic studies).

Therefore, that sub-optimal effectiveness of the surveillance in wild birds cannot be considered in line with provisions laid down in Articles 26(2) and (4) and 27 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429, on the need to design and apply surveillance in a way that is appropriate and proportionate to the objectives pursued and to the risk factors involved in order to ensure the timely detection of the presence of the targeted disease. In doing that, the competent authority shall as well comply with EU requirements establishing the Union surveillance programme for HPAI, as laid down in Articles 3(1)(a) and (b)(i), 4(1)(b)(i) and 10(2) of, and Annex II to Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/689.

Although the authorities have made efforts to increase the sensitivity of surveillance in both wild birds and domestic poultry, surveillance in the former was only partially effective as an early warning system to better prevent the outbreaks in both epizootics and to confirm epidemiological hypothesis on the source of infection in affected establishments.

Wild birds can also be exposed to virus from infected poultry farms. Having positive cases in poultry will result in information in media and direct to farms in proximity, thus additional findings in wild birds are not needed as a basis for activities to raise awareness and increase biosecurity.

recommendations.text: To take appropriate action to improve the effectiveness of the biosecurity measures applied by operators of poultry establishments, by: a) evaluating their suitability to mitigate the prevailing risk factors involved in the areas where they are situated according to the local circumstances and practices, and b) applying effective and appropriate official controls on a risk basis and with appropriate frequency to verify their proper application. Articles 10(1)(a)(iii), (b) and (c), (4) and (5), and 11(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429. Article 5(1)(a) and 9 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. , and 27

citations.text: When reviewing one of the HPAI outbreaks, confirmed on 2 March 2021 in an establishment keeping pheasants for game re-stocking, the audit team noted that in January, i.e., once the SBA had raised the alert concerning the high risk of incursion of the disease, the business operator responsible for the establishment had re-captured previously released birds from the wild. The district veterinarians who dealt with the outbreak were aware of this practice, as they confirmed that it is common during that period of the year in several establishments from the area. However, neither them or other staff of the SBA had investigated the potential risk associated with that activity, and they had not taken either any action to prevent additional outbreaks in these specific establishments.

The SBA delegated inspections on biosecurity in establishments to the poultry meat and eggs sectoral associations. However, examples like the one explained in the previous point prove that at least some parts of the poultry industry had not adapted disease preventive measures properly to mitigate the specific risks associated with the presence of HPAI in wild birds in accordance with the requirements established by the SBA, as required until 20 April 2021 by Commission Decision 2018/1136 and, since that date, by provisions laid down in Articles 10(1)(a)(iii), (b) and (c), (4) and (5), and 11(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429.

In addition, the competent authorities had not adapted their official controls, or their procedures and/or arrangements to verify their effectiveness, to ensure that the biosecurity measures applied by the industry were suitable, implemented in compliance with their instructions, and that the inspections carried out by the sector itself were effective to achieve that. This is not line with Articles 5(1)(a), 9(1) and 33(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Surveillance

The results of most of the epidemiological enquiries indicated that the outbreaks were very likely caused by a separate primary introduction of the HPAI virus from wild birds. This was confirmed later by the SVA with phylogenetic analyses. Some epidemiological enquiries underlined weaknesses related to the application of biosecurity measures to prevent the introduction of HPAI. However, the SBA had not adequately investigated the possible influence of those weaknesses as a cause of infection, even recurrent in both epizootics, in certain establishments (e.g., in the turkey production sector).

The lack of a system to adequately verify compliance of poultry establishments with HPAI preventive measures precludes that the SBA obtains accurate and up-to-date information on the actual implementation and effectiveness of their HPAI preventive policy. Despite evidence on the inappropriate application of, and insufficient compliance with national requirements on biosecurity in poultry establishments affected by the HPAI epizootics, the SBA failed to correct those shortcomings. This resulted in an unmitigated high risk of infection in certain types of establishments, which contributed to some of the outbreaks and, in certain cases, to recurrent infections in the same establishments in both epizootics.

The SBA allowed repopulation in affected establishments only after the final cleaning and disinfection was carried out. SBA staff verified establishments' compliance with 20 national requirements on biosecurity measures and that they were suitable to minimise the risks of introduction of HPAI. The audit team saw some examples where they gave recommendations to operators to address weaknesses identified in that respect. In one of the cases checked, an establishment that was infected in both epizootics, at the time of the second outbreak the operator had not addressed some of the recommendations given by SBA staff after the checks carried out after the first one. Representatives of both the SBA and the SVA acknowledged that shortcoming. The SBA informed the audit team that they were in the process of evaluating and reinforcing those checks on biosecurity in poultry establishments (see section 5.1.1.1, and the associated conclusion, on weaknesses related to application and verification of preventive measures).

The project will be finished by the end of 2023. recommendations.text: To make appropriate arrangements to perform adequate epidemiological enquiries and accelerate and document the analysis of their results in case of suspicion and confirmation of HPAI so that the competent authorities can take appropriate preventive and control measures adapted to the causes and the risks of spread of the disease. Articles 55(1)(e) and (f), 56(a)(ii), 57(2), and 62(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429. Article 8(3) and (4), 13(1)(a) and 22(2) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687. , and

citations.text: The district veterinarians responsible for the areas where the suspect cases were notified initiated the epidemiological enquiries at the time of suspicion. In most cases, they finished with them shortly after the disease had been confirmed. But some of them were incomplete, not providing all relevant epidemiological information/data, e.g., they did not include information on other establishments of the same owner, often sharing their machinery, which they did not identify as contact holdings. In addition, they had not considered properly the risk of virus transmission associated with some relevant contacts and epidemiological links (e.g., delivery of feed, trucks from a rendering plant and trucks collecting table eggs), which they did not follow to identify contact establishments and place them under supervision to rule out the potential spread of the disease. Therefore, although those enquiries aimed to obtain the relevant information required by Article 57(2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429, they did not achieve that consistently.

District veterinarians provided the collected information to the SBA. The SBA frequently relayed it to the SVA, which analysed it promptly in some cases. SBA and SVA experts visited most of the outbreaks to further evaluate the epidemiological situation on site, but they did that only once the establishments had been depopulated and the carcasses dispatched for their disposal5. That precluded that those experts could obtain important information on the routine operation of the establishment and from their own evaluation of the evolution of the disease in the affected poultry present in the establishment.

In some cases, the outcome of the analyses carried out by the SVA and the SBA served to establish the most likely time window for the infection of the flocks, the duration of the incubation period, and to obtain other relevant epidemiological information. However, those results had not been adequately documented to show how the SBA and/or the SVA used them for a complete analysis of the likely routes of introduction of 5 In their response to the draft report the CA stated that these HPAI outbreaks occurred during a time when there were national restrictions on movements due to the Covid-19 pandemic, therefore it was not possible to visit the outbreaks to an extent that otherwise would have been done. 8 the virus in the affected establishments and of its possible spread, and to identify quickly contact establishments. Therefore, the authorities could not fulfil all the objectives of the epidemiological enquiries to inform their decisions on the application of control measures to contain the HPAI outbreaks, as provided for in Articles 55(1)(e) and (f), 56(a)(ii), 57(2), and 62(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429, and Articles 14(1), 17 and 18(2) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687.

There were cases where district veterinarians had to prioritise other official tasks, for example, preparation and performing of killing of poultry and disposal of carcasses in affected establishments. That delayed often completion of the epidemiological inquiries for the same establishments. The audit team confirmed that in a large laying hen establishment infected at the beginning of 2021, as the district veterinarian could only complete the epidemiological enquiry 18 days after confirmation of the disease. That establishment had multiple houses, some separated by considerable distance (e.g., separating the area with houses keeping pullets from those keeping laying hens). The SBA had decided after an evaluation carried out months before the outbreak that, considering the husbandry practices applied, there were multiple epidemiological units6 in the establishment. At the time of the outbreak, the SBA decided to grant accordingly a derogation as provided for in Article 14 of Council Directive 2005/94/EC, applicable at the time, to not kill the poultry from the epidemiological units not affected initially (since 21 April 2021, this derogation is provided by Article 13 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687).

In that case, the district veterinarian was in constant contact with the SBA and provided initially some epidemiologically relevant information on the establishment, but the fact that the full enquiry was delayed precluded that both the SBA and the SVA obtained all the necessary information to fully analyse the situation and adapt accordingly the measures taken (e.g. testing of other epidemiological units, further restrictions in their movements). The SBA did not consider necessary consulting the SVA before deciding on granting that derogation.

However, as mentioned before (section 5.1.1.2), not all contact establishments were identified or duly followed up. That is not in line with EU requirements laid down in Article 62(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429, and Article 18(2) of Delegated Regulation 11 (EU) 2020/687. Conclusions on early detection, handling of suspicion and confirmation of HPAI

The inconsistent and slow analysis in many cases of the data and information collected by district veterinarians during the epidemiological enquiries, alongside the often inadequate documentation of its outcome, made it difficult for the SBA to take timely and appropriate risk-based control measures (e.g., identifying contact establishments, granting of derogations for separate epidemiological units and for movements in restricted zones). That slowed down the response to the disease, which was not as effective as it should have been to limit the impact of the outbreaks.

However, as described in sections 5.1.1.2 to 4, certain limitations in the provision of quick and adequate epidemiological information from the affected establishments precluded that both the expert group and the national disease control centre could analyse all necessary data to advice on the application of some disease control measures (e.g., handling of separate epidemiological units in some establishments, granting of some derogations).

District veterinarians demonstrated good knowledge about the measures they had to apply to respond to HPAI outbreaks, with some exceptions related to carrying out and evaluating epidemiological enquiries. In general, they carried out their tasks timely; however, there were instances where due to overload they had to prioritise some activities over other and they could not apply some of the required disease control measures (e.g., prioritise killing over epidemiological enquiries, which resulted in delays to perform the latter, they could not visit hobby/non-commercial establishments situated in some protection zones, they could not supervise cleaning and disinfection activities in some cases). The SBA did not have flexible arrangements and sufficient human resources to react quickly and address those gaps. That was not in line with requirements laid down in Articles 13(1)(a) and 43(2)(c)(iv) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 on responsibilities of the competent authorities to have an effective organisation and access to personnel to apply disease control measures timely and effectively, and on application of the contingency plan for HPAI. 5.2.5 Availability of equipment and materials

However, in doing that, the SBA did not carry out a proper risk assessment at the time of the outbreak, taking into account the results of the epidemiological enquiry (which was not yet done at the time of the decision) and the possibility to obtain first favourable results in laboratory examinations to exclude the circulation of the HPAI virus in still asymptomatic poultry.

In addition, the lack of updated relevant epidemiological information from the first infected unit precluded excluding that at least during the monitoring period of 21 days before the confirmation of the disease, the epidemiological units in which the disease had 7 See for example: Grant M, Bröjer C, Zohari S, Nöremark M, Uhlhorn H, Jansson DS. In addition, still during the 2020/21 epizootic, the SBA applied the same approach in another establishment keeping breeding poultry, considering some of the houses as separate epidemiological units, after the disease was confirmed in one of the units. They did not only grant the derogation to not kill the poultry from the not (yet) affected units, but also allowed the dispatch of several consignments of hatching eggs from them to other establishments in Sweden (see also section 5.1.3.4 concerning that derogation). Those decisions were taken without carrying out a proper risk assessment and without considering either the epidemiological and laboratory analysis information mentioned in the previous point to exclude the possible circulation of the HPAI virus in the other units of the establishment.

In the above cases, the disease was detected eventually in other epidemiological units, and all birds remaining on the establishments were subsequently killed. The few remaining units not yet clinically affected were preventively culled. However, the SBA did not take any samples to rule out the infection in those units, as required at the time by Article 10(3) of Directive 2005/94/EC and point 8.2 in Chapter IV of the Annex to Commission Decision 2006/437/EC. Nor did the SBA take any action to trace and destroy hatching eggs already dispatched to hatcheries in non-affected areas of the country from these preventively killed birds. All in all, the process to grant those derogations was not in line with requirements laid down in Article 14 of Directive 2005/94/EC, which are since 21 April 2021 laid down and reinforced in Article 13(1) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687.

The measures applied immediately upon confirmation of HPAI outbreaks during both epizootics were adequate in most cases and helped to contain the spread of the disease. However, during the 2020/21 epizootic, the SBA granted certain derogations that postponed the killing of poultry in epidemiological units of affected establishments considered as separate. Those decisions proved to be not only unjustified, as most of those units got eventually infected by the same HPAI virus, but were also not based on a proper risk assessment to exclude any risk of spread of the disease, as required by EU legislation. Despite that, there was no evidence that those situations had contributed to spread HPAI from the relevant establishments. 5.1.2 Diagnosis of HPAI

Before they could grant the derogation for those movements, district veterinarians performed checks on the health status of the poultry kept in the relevant establishments. 15 Beyond that, the SBA did not require any pre-movement sampling and laboratory testing since they did not consider it necessary. They argued that the HPAI viruses circulating in Sweden during both epizootics caused obvious clinical symptoms and high mortality in the poultry species kept, and thus, that they were easily and quickly detectable during the clinical examinations and checks on production records their staff carried out (e.g., no establishments with ducks or geese involved).

The audit team reviewed several examples where a derogation was granted. One of them, happening before 21 April 2021, involved dispatching hatching eggs from units of breeding establishments where a case of HPAI was confirmed, that the SBA considered as separate epidemiological units (see more details in section 5.1.1.3). However, they did that without taking and analyse first the standard samples from each of the production units involved in that activity, as required by point 8.10(c) of Chapter IV of the Annex to Commission Decision (EC) 2006/437, in accordance with the requirements of Article 26(1)(a) of Directive 2005/94/EC (applicable at the time of the outbreak).

In another case, happening in December 2021, the SBA granted a derogation to move poultry to a slaughterhouse from two establishments belonging to the same operator, in whose third establishment they had just confirmed an outbreak of HPAI (two days before). One of those two establishments was located in the protection zone established after the outbreak, less than two kilometres from the affected one, whereas the second one was within the surveillance zone. All three establishments shared some machinery, and the operator visited them regularly. Although all that evidence indicated that those movements could represent a high risk of spreading the disease, the SBA allowed them without carrying out a proper risk assessment and applying additional risk mitigating measures, e.g., laboratory examination with favourable results of samples taken from poultry kept in those establishments, including from the animals to be moved.

The competent authority granted some derogations to move animals and products of animal origin from restricted zones without adequately ensuring that they would not endanger disease control, as required by EU legislation. Nevertheless, there was no evidence that those situations had any impact on the further spread of the disease or in delaying its containment. 5.1.4 Animal depopulation for the purpose of disease control 5.1.4.1 Animal welfare considerations

However, as described in sections 5.1.1.2 to 4, certain limitations in the provision of quick and adequate epidemiological information from the affected establishments precluded that both the expert group and the national disease control centre could analyse all necessary data to advice on the application of some disease control measures (e.g., handling of separate epidemiological units in some establishments, granting of some derogations).

The disease control centres established at national and local level during the epizootics, in particular during the one in 2020/21, coordinated the response to most of the outbreaks effectively. However, they lacked some necessary information to take important decisions related to specific outbreaks. Although those decisions could have had important consequences (e.g., transmission of the disease locally, or elsewhere in the country via derogated movements), the low density of poultry in the affected areas and the low risk associated with commodities allowed to leave the restricted zones, helped to prevent the spread of the disease.

citations.text: In most cases, collection and disposal of killed poultry operated swiftly and without delay. However, in the case of a large establishment affected by an outbreak in 2021, the authorities lacked sufficient collection and processing capacity. This was due to the exceptionally large number of poultry carcasses and an exceptionally large number of eggs. To cope with the situation and keep on killing the poultry, the SBA opted for the temporary storage of those ABP in specially designed big bags on the establishment until they were collected and processed as described above along the following four months. During that time, the SBA paid special attention to the application of biosecurity measures to prevent the spread of infection from the material stored in the establishment, which was situated in an area with low density of establishments, e.g., the closest one was 7 km apart.

The shortcomings highlighted in the previous point are not in line with requirements of Articles 13(1)(a), 43(2)(c)(i) and (iii), and 61(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429, on the responsibilities of the competent authorities to have access to adequate facilities to take the necessary disease control measures, including disposal of animals that may contribute to the spread of a category A disease in the event of an animal health crisis, such as the 2020/21 HPAI epizootic.

At the time of the audit, and despite the lessons learnt from the case mentioned above, the contingency plan for HPAI had not yet been updated to anticipate and deal with such exceptional situation. However, the SBA amended their procedures to speed up the disposal of ABP from the average poultry establishment affected by a HPAI outbreak, e.g., starting preparations for collection and disposal of carcasses already at the time of suspicion. Furthermore, they intend to explore other options to strengthen their preparedness, e.g., to transfer partially the responsibility for disposal of carcasses to business operators, who should develop a specific contingency plan for their establishments with that purpose. Conclusions on animal depopulation for the purpose of disease control

The authorities had taken adequate steps and made the necessary logistical arrangements to ensure sufficient capacity to collect and dispose safely of the carcases of dead and killed poultry in the event of outbreaks of HPAI affecting establishments of average size and not occurring in spatiotemporal clusters. However, that preparedness did not factor in the possibility of an outbreak in some exceptionally large establishments, where significant delays in applying those measures increased for weeks the risk of spread of the disease. Although the low density of poultry in the affected area mitigated that risk and no additional outbreak was confirmed in it, the authorities have not yet upscaled their preparedness to address that shortcoming. 5.1.5 Cleaning and disinfection

The SBA externalised the application of the preliminary cleaning and disinfection in affected establishments to private contractors, who, in most cases, did it within short deadlines once the poultry were killed and the carcasses disposed of. There were cases where the authorities had to postpone the application of both preliminary and final cleaning and disinfection because of the limited capacity of some of those contractors or as a consequence of delays in removal of dead bodies or killed animals. Thus, in some instances, because of those delays, the SBA lifted the restrictions in surveillance zones without having applied first the final cleaning and disinfection (see also section 5.1.6).

In a large establishment affected by an outbreak at the beginning of 2021, the SBA initially questioned the efficacy of applying the preliminary disinfection due to unfavourable weather conditions (low temperatures and snow fall), as they considered that the biocidal available was not going to be effective. After further consultation with the SVA, they decided to proceed with the disinfection. In addition, the final cleaning and disinfection was delayed for more than four months due to the presence of contaminated materials (for more see section 5.1.4.2).

Staff from the SBA at central level and some of the district veterinarians met confirmed that they had not supervised implementation of cleaning and disinfection activities in all affected establishments, as required by Article 48(a) of Directive 2005/94/EC (before 21 April 2021) and Article 57(2) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687 (since 21 April 2021). Conclusions on cleaning and disinfection

The competent authorities ensured that adequate cleaning and disinfection of most affected establishments contributed to the elimination of residual infection, except where the presence of contaminated materials precluded them to do so and caused delays, and when they could not supervise application of those measures. Although those 19 shortcomings increased temporarily the risk of spreading the infection in certain areas, there was no evidence that it had happened. 5.1.6 Lifting of restrictions

The fact that the SBA decided in several cases to lift the restrictions in surveillance zones before having implemented and/or supervised the final cleaning and disinfection on establishments affected by HPAI outbreaks was not in line with Article 68(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429. Conclusions on lifting of restrictions

The SBA did not ensure that the objective of applying the final cleaning and disinfection on establishments affected by HPAI outbreaks, i.e., to minimise the risk of spread of the disease, was achieved in all cases before discontinuing the application of control measures in restricted zones. Although that non-compliance with EU rules increased temporarily that risk, there was no evidence that it had materialised in further outbreaks of the disease. 5.1.7 Repopulation of affected holdings

citations.text: The SBA has not fully updated the contingency plan for HPAI in recent years, despite the recent epizootics and the recurrent risk of incursion via wild birds of HPAI in EU Member States. They have been developing for several years a new version of that contingency plan trying to adapt it to the one they developed for foot-and-mouth disease, but several parts still need to be amended and further developed, including some operational manuals.

In the last three years, there has been no simulation exercise on HPAI to test the emergency preparedness system. Nevertheless, the authorities provided evidence on several actions introduced in their animal health emergency preparedness system as a result of the lessons learnt from the 2020/2021 and 2021/2022 HPAI epizootics. Those 21 actions aim to increase the effectiveness of their system, e.g., on conducting of epidemiological enquiries, new arrangements for disposal of carcasses, on killing of poultry, including provisions on preventive killing, on raising awareness, and to streamline certain administrative procedures.

The improvements mentioned in the previous point go in the right direction, but the situation found at the time of both epizootics cannot be considered in line with EU requirements laid down in Article 62 of Directive 2005/94/EC (before 21 April 2021) and Article 43(2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 (since 21 April 2021), on the matters that contingency plans should at least cover. The persistent delay in updating the plan is not in line with EU requirements laid down in Article 62(5) of the said directive (before 21 April 2021) Article 43(1) of the said regulation (since 21 April 2021), and precluded the competent authorities to apply all necessary disease control measures during both HPAI epizootics in accordance with Chapter II to IV of Directive 2005/94/EC (before 21 April 2021) and Article 4 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687 (since 21 April 2021). 5.2.2 Registration of poultry holdings ­ Areas with high density of poultry

District veterinarians demonstrated good knowledge about the measures they had to apply to respond to HPAI outbreaks, with some exceptions related to carrying out and evaluating epidemiological enquiries. In general, they carried out their tasks timely; however, there were instances where due to overload they had to prioritise some activities over other and they could not apply some of the required disease control measures (e.g., prioritise killing over epidemiological enquiries, which resulted in delays to perform the latter, they could not visit hobby/non-commercial establishments situated in some protection zones, they could not supervise cleaning and disinfection activities in some cases). The SBA did not have flexible arrangements and sufficient human resources to react quickly and address those gaps. That was not in line with requirements laid down in Articles 13(1)(a) and 43(2)(c)(iv) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 on responsibilities of the competent authorities to have an effective organisation and access to personnel to apply disease control measures timely and effectively, and on application of the contingency plan for HPAI. 5.2.5 Availability of equipment and materials

The authorities have not fully updated and verified the functionality of the contingency plan and related operational manuals for HPAI in recent years, despite the recent epizootics and the recurrent risk of incursion via wild birds of HPAI. That missed opportunity to adequately reinforce all important components of their emergency preparedness system, including up-to-date training of district veterinarians, had a detrimental effect on the timeliness, selection and effectiveness of some of the measures applied to control the disease outbreaks, and could have had worse consequences resulting in the further spread of HPAI.

recommendations.text: Ensure that official controls on authorised operators and operators seeking authorisation should address and record if the applicant/authorised operator: has identified and monitors critical points in their production process and conducts meticulous examinations in line with Ar- ticle 87(3) and 90(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 prior to issuing plant passports, keeps relevant records on the monitor- ing of critical control points and meticulous examinations for at least three years as required by Articles 87(3) and 90(1) of Reg- ulation (EU) 2016/2031, has access to the information on modalities of visual inspections and information on the best practices and preventive measures to prevent pest presences required by Article 2(b) and (c) of the Regulation (EU) 2019/827

citations.text: The audit team noted that compliance of professional operators with the requirements of Article 1(b)(d) of Regulation (EU) 2019/827, such as competence to conduct plant health examinations and to apply best practices and measures to prevent the presence and spread of plant pests, is not verified during the authorisation process. This is not in line with Article 89(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031.

For compliance with Article 2 (a)(b)(c) of Regulation (EU) 2019/827, SBA has provided operators some information on their website, mainly for priority pests and for some EU quarantine pests such as regulated potato pests. For other pests, links to the EPPO global database were made available (information is in English only). The CA has not provided operators information on modalities of visual inspections as required by Article (2)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2019/827 and information on best practices and measures to prevent pest presences as required by Article (2)(c) of the same Regulation. 5.3.2 Official supervision of professional operators and verification of their actions

As inspection guidelines and checklists do not require verification of the authorised op- erators' compliance with the requirements of Articles 87 and 90 on the appropriateness of authorised operators' examinations and obligation to keep records on examinations, compliance with these requirements was not included in any of the observed inspections. This is not in line with Article 92(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. Conclusions on authorisation and supervision of professional operators for issuing plant passports:

The system of authorisation of professional operators to issue plant passports follows rules established in EU legislation. However, the CA has neither provided authorised operators with the information needed to carry out meticulous inspections independent- ly and at critical points, nor has it required them to keep records of such inspections. Moreover, there is no requirement in the guidelines for the CA to verify compliance to the abovementioned criteria. These shortcomings increase the risk that operators do not carry out their inspections meticulously, and that they place plants on the market, in- fested with regulated pests.

Operators met by the audit team stated that they check their plants constantly as they go about their work, even though formally not required to do so by the SBA. However, as operators visited had never documented this activity, as required by Article 87(3)(d) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031, the audit team could not verify that authorised operators conduct meticulous examinations in line with Article 87(3) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 prior to issuing plant passports. In addition, only one of the operators met by 8 the audit team had defined their critical points and the list of pests for monitoring pur- poses as required by Article 90(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. No records are kept on monitoring by authorised operators. The reason for not undertaking this task is the lack of specific requirements and official controls by the SBA as stated in point 27 in section 5.3.2. 5.4.2 Examinations by competent authorities including the verification of examinations carried out by authorised operators

The lack of evidence that authorised operators carry out meticulous examinations prior to issuing plant passports, and the absence of controls to verify this, provides insuffi- cient assurance that plants for which plant passports have been granted in Sweden are free of relevant pests.

The official controls on sales through distance contracts are undertaken at those opera- tors who had registered this specific activity in the national plant health registry. The of- ficial controls at operators issuing plant passports are undertaken as described under sec- tions 5.3 to 5.5, with the inspection scope focusing mainly on the format and attachment of the plant passports and traceability. Authorised operators' compliance with the re- quirements of Articles 87 and 90 on the appropriateness of authorised operators' exami- nations and obligation to keep records on examinations is not verified by the CA. The inspection frequency for 2022 and 2023 was met and no non-compliances were reported regarding plant passports and traceability. Conclusions on official controls on movement of plants and plant products with plant passports

Similar to the official controls at other operators authorised to issue plant passports, the controls at the operators that sell their products through distance contracts provide in- sufficient assurance that plants for which plant passports have been granted in Sweden are free of relevant pests.

responses.response: The competent authority (SBA) will ensure that the authorised operators and operators seeking authorisation prior to issuing nt passports conduct and properly record the meticulous examinations. The SBA will ensure that those operators identify itor critical points within their production processes. This will be achieved through an amendment of the SBA guidance, instructions and check list for official controls as well as the performance of the official controls themselves, in order to achieve better compliance with the requirements in Article 87(3) and 90(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. The SBA plans to achieve those adaptations in a phased pproach, as follows: 1 - By the end of the year, the SBA will have developed relevant information with the intention to start disseminating it via the web and through direct communication channels to authorized operators. 2 - By the end of the year the SBA will have adjusted its guidance on controls in order to enable corresponding adjustments of the control instructions and check list for 2025. 3 - The controls will be carried out accordingly after the guidance on controls, control instruction and check list documents are amended, if possible
