recommendations.text: To ensure that a suitable procedure is in place to monitor and verify that official controls in slaughterhouses are carried out effectively and appropriately in accordance with Article 5(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: In the other two regions, including the one where all the establishments visited by the audit team were located, no regular or structured on-site monitoring or supervision visits take place to confirm that the OVs carry out their duties satisfactorily, consistently and in accordance with the SFA guidelines and legislation.

Other than in one region of the country (where it is currently being carried out on a trial basis), there is no regular or structured on-site supervision of the establishments' official staff taking place to confirm that the OVs and OAs carry out the controls in the slaughterhouses correctly, consistently and in accordance with the SFA guidelines and legislation. The existing system is based on remote support and analysis of indicators. Although this is useful for identifying trends and differences between regions or even establishments, it is not suitable way to recognise individual deficiencies. As a result of the design of the system, some non-compliances or failures in the delivery of official controls cannot be identified and resolved.

Although the majority of the PMI procedures were conducted satisfactorily, the audit team identified several aspects that were not in compliance with the legislation: 11 · Carcases passed as fit for human consumption by the OV/OA team before the removal of some pathological lesions; this removal/trimming was the responsibility of the FBO's staff and occurred after the PMI was performed by the OV/OA and the carcase was health marked. No further checks were carried out by the OV/OA to ensure that the rectification of the carcase had been performed satisfactorily; · Lack of lockable facilities for the refrigerated storage of detained meat in one of the establishments visited. Post-mortem inspection - poultry

PMI procedures only covered the external surface of the carcases and the offal. Neither the OV nor the FBO staff carried out a cavity inspection of the poultry carcases as required by Article 12 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. 12 5.3.2 Official controls over food business operators' obligations Food Chain Information (FCI) and animal identification Legal requirements Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004 in conjunction with its Annex II Section III and Article 9 and 10, 40, 41 42 and 43.1 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. Findings

The audit team observed several unhygienic practices taking place during the visits, some of them systematically occurring in several establishments. They included the overuse of drop hoses by operatives to clean themselves and the equipment, causing a risk of cross-contamination to nearby carcases by uncontrolled splashing. It was noted that staff could not make use of apron washes or other suitable alternatives as no apron washing cabinets were available in the majority of the slaughterhouses visited. Also, some water pipes and hand-wash basins on working platforms were not properly ducted, which facilitated the pooling of water and thereby created a risk of contamination of dirty water splashing onto carcases and offal. These two issues had not been identified or enforced by the OVs. Microbiological criteria Legal requirements Articles 35 and 36 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. Commission Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. recommendations.text: To ensure that risk-based official controls take into account the reliability and the results of operators' own controls during the risk assessment of feed business operators.

citations.text: The SBA has a risk-based planning approach for its official inspections. The risk assessment is based on different risk factors (e.g., the type of activity(s) registered, the quantity of production, results of previous official controls). The final score is based on a mathematical formula which converts the risk factors into numerical values and provides the risk class for each of the FeBOs (score between 1 and 7) which determines the inspection frequency for each FeBO. The frequency varies between once every 7 years (very low) to three times per year (high). FeBOs dealing with medicated feed are also included in the risk-based planning. The audit team noted that the planning for the risk assessment of official inspections does not take into account the reliability and results of own controls performed by FeBOs which is not in line with the requirements laid down in Article 9(1)(d) to Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

The planning of inspections is based on several appropriate risk-related factors but the reliability of operators `own controls is not considered and is a notable gap in an otherwise well-functioning risk-based planning process. While official inspections are carried out on all operators with an appropriate frequency, the effectiveness of these inspections, and thus of the overall system governing the production of feed, is weakened by several shortcomings in their execution. These relate to the inspectors' assessment of feed business operators' tests to verify that the measures they have taken to minimise cross contamination has been effective, and checks on the operators' adherence with the requirements for veterinary prescriptions and the labels of medicated feeds. 5.2.2 Sampling and analysis 5.2.2.1 Planning of official sampling

recommendations.legal_basis: point 3 of the section "Production" of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005 and point 2 of the section 4 "Quality control" of Annex I to Regulation (EU) 2019/4.

citations.text: Verification of establishments' tests to assess the measures taken to minimise cross- contamination, required by part 2(b) of section "Facilities and equipment" of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005, forms part of the inspections, when applicable. In two establishments visited, tests to assess the extent of cross contamination were carried out twice per year and the test results were acceptable. However, in one establishment the FeBO`s written instruction on the testing method was unclear and the implementation of the tests was not in line with the scientific requirements (e.g., the place of sampling, the number of samples taken, the mixing of samples and the first mix to be sampled). The other establishment used two different types of coccidiostats. The tests carried out concerned one of the coccidiostats. The feed inspectors met, were able to assess some parts of these test procedures, but experienced difficulties in comprehensively assessing the procedures and the results of the cross-contamination tests.

In one establishment visited the FeBO tested the cleaning (flushing) batch between the production of feed with coccidiostats (narasin) and subsequently without coccidiostats. The FeBO tested the coccidiostat concentration of the first, second and third subsequent mixing following the production of feed with coccidiostats. The concentration of the carry-over of coccidiostats was higher in these mixes than the maximum level described in point 7 of Annex I Section VII of Directive 2002/32/EC. The FeBO did not place these contaminated feeds on the market but used these feeds during the production of complete feeds for broilers containing narasin. Based on the recipe of this type of complete feed, the narasin concentration in the final feed was higher than the maximum limit in Commission Regulation (EC) No 545/2006. This absence of regular checks is not in line with the requirements laid down in point 2 of Section 4 of Annex I to Regulation (EU) No 2019/4.

citations.text: Regarding the above instructions, the auditors found that moisture analysis, when required, is to be performed by a yet-to-be determined external accredited laboratory. recommendations.text: To ensure that the residue control plans for pharmacologically active substances are implemented in line with planned arrangements.
recommendations.legal_basis: Article 4 of Regulation (EU) 2022/1646 and Article 9(2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: The implementation of the plan largely meets the NRCP requirements with respect to the minimum sampling frequencies (24) for 2023, covers the full calendar year for most commodities, and is on schedule for 2024. The SFA laboratory staff, aided by sample reception assistants, monitor whether the expected samples have been taken and have arrived at the laboratory and take action if this is not the case. In 2023, there was a greater than 100% achievement rate for some commodities due to a misunderstanding, i.e., samples were taken to match the number of analyses and not the number of planned samples of a specific matrix. The sampling rate for pharmacologically active substances (all commodities) was also greater than 100% at slaughterhouses but ranged from 74- 108% on farms, depending on the commodity, with no explanation having been provided for the 74% sampling achievement rate on pig farms. The sampling achievement rate was 92% at egg collection centres, 84% at fish farms and 78% at honey collection centres. Difficulties in getting the samples from the CABs was provided as the explanation for the shortfall in fish samples. No explanation was provided for the honey sample shortfall. All sampling reports examined by the audit team in situ contained the information required in EU legislation (25). 5.2 Implementation of the national randomised surveillance plan for residues of pharmacologically active substances

audits.title: Plant Protection Products

recommendations.text: To ensure that: · The official controls include all PPP operators in the chain of marketing and use of PPPs as required by Article 9(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, · The Competent Authority keeps or has access to an up-to-date lists of operators as required by Article 10(2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Recommendation is based upon conclusions No 55

citations.text: The SCA uses a list of first-tier suppliers derived from the companies listed in the SCA's product register. The SCA acknowledged that the list is not complete as regards first-tier suppliers as the operators that have registered themselves are not always the operators responsible in Sweden. Moreover, the information collected about the operators´ activities in the PPP register is very basic (only name and address of the headquarters of the company) and limits the planning of controls (see paragraph 64). In addition to the product register, the SCA may also consult the SCA's pesticide register which contains information on all PPPs that are authorised or have been authorised in Sweden.

Regarding marketing and agricultural users, each MUP is responsible for maintaining its own register/list. The audit team visited four MUPs and all stated that they are working with lists. All MUPs acknowledged that the list of operators is a work in progress. It is updated with the information they get from their activities, complaints gathered during 8 visits carried out in the framework of projects intended for other purposes, etc. They acknowledged that the lists may not include all operators relevant for the controls of PPPs. Training for acquiring PPP certificates

The CABs organise training programmes for operators and advisors. This training results in the issuance of certificates that qualify individuals for activities related to the distribution, sale, or use of PPPs. The SBA maintains a list of those who have successfully completed the training. Planning of official controls on marketing and distribution of PPPs

The inspection covered most aspects relevant for the official control of PPPs. The SCA checked the labelling of seven products, asked for the training certificate of staff and verified some of the records kept by the company. However, the warehouse and re-packer facilities, mentioned above, were not part of the inspection (see also paragraph 36). Controls at retailers/distributors of PPPs

The audit team noted good examples of collaborations between the SCA and Customs. Customs sent 11 inquiries to the SCA in 2023, and 3 illegal PPPs were detected as a result. In 2024, 46 inquiries were sent, and 39 illegal PPPs were detected. Conclusions on controls on the marketing of plant protection products

recommendations.text: Ensure that official controls on the marketing and use of PPPs are performed regularly, with appropriate frequency and to ensure that the frequency of inspections at operators is decided upon using objective criteria that consider the risk of inappropriate PPP usage and the results of monitoring programmes as necessary. This is to comply with Article 9(1) and 24(1) and (2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Recommendation is based upon conclusions No 55 and 56

citations.text: MUPs are responsible for controls at non-agricultural users. In one MUP visited, inspections are determined by an assessment following the guidance issued by the Environmental Agency and also on experience gained from previous controls. For example, golf courses are classified as low risk, with a frequency of one visit every 5 years. The MUP stated that due to limited resources, visits do not always cover all aspects relevant for the use of PPPs. Sometimes inspections are part of projects that focus on only one or a few specific aspects. For example, the previous inspection focused on whether the required distances between spots where PPPs were applied and ditches and water courses were respected. In another MUP, golf courses are inspected every other year. Inspections are typically announced in advance.

The audit team found that inspection of farmers has not been consistently conducted in recent years, according to information provided by the MUPs. The MUPs reported difficulties in meeting the inspection frequency recommended by the SCA and the SBA due to resource constraints. In one MUP visited, out of approximately 350 farmers, only three were inspected in 2023, and those inspections were solely for fertilizer controls. In 2024, only 11 farms were inspected, despite an annual target of around 55. Another MUP visited indicated that they do not maintain specific statistics on the controls of PPP users. 10 They can provide numbers for the total inspections conducted, but these may not align with the planned or expected inspections specifically related to PPP use. This approach does not fully comply with Articles 9(1) and 24(1) and (2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

The water framework directive results are taken into account for controls. However, the results of the national pesticide residue programme mentioned are not always taken into account for the planning of inspections. This is not in line with Article 24(2)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The audit team considered that the results that show use of unauthorised PPPs, as well as those showing exceedance of maximum residue levels for authorised PPPs would be relevant for follow-up during inspections.

Inspections of users are announced, normally four weeks in advance. Inspections to follow up on problems found previously can be "unannounced" (although warning can be given 24 hours in advance). The CAs stated that the advance notice is necessary, as growers are often not present on farms. This is not in line with Article 9(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Moreover, advance notice could compromise inspection effectiveness by allowing operators ample time to alter conditions at their premises, such as removing unauthorised PPPs. Planning of sampling for formulation analyses of PPPs

There is guidance for MUPs to determine inspection frequency based on risk criteria. However, the lack of a well-defined and comprehensive list of operators for control, the currently reduced frequency and limited scope of routine inspections may reduce the general effectiveness of these controls. In addition, the sampling procedure is not in line with the official control regulation.

recommendations.text: To define conditions and establish criteria for when prior notice to operators marketing and using PPPs would be necessary and duly justified for the official controls to be carried out. This is to comply with Article 9 (4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: MUPs are in charge of controls of operators marketing PPPs not covered by the SCA controls, i.e. retailers, wholesalers and distributors. The SCA, in collaboration with the SAB has prepared guidance for risk assessment and determining the frequency of the visits. The MUPs may use this guidance but are not obliged to follow it. In principle, inspections carried out by the MUPs of marketing of PPPs are unannounced. 9

Agricultural users are selected for inspections based on risk criteria outlined in the guidance prepared by the SBA. One of the key criteria is farm size. For example, farms smaller than 50 ha must be inspected at least every five years and larger ones every three or four years. The MUPs also consider the results of previous controls, adjusting the frequency accordingly. These criteria mainly apply to arable crops, while different risk criteria apply for other type of users The MUP stated that for inspections of greenhouses, they follow the Swedish Environmental Code, focusing primarily on structural integrity and checking for potential leakages, rather than concentrating on PPP usage. This approach deviates from the primary purpose of these controls, which should be to verify the use of PPPs by operators. This is not in line with Articles 9(1) and 24(1) and (2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

The SCA develops an annual sampling plan based on risk criteria. These criteria follow the EU draft 2018 guidance document, version 1, and include: 50% of the products selected are those with high sales volumes, 25% are high-risk products with, for example, a history of non-compliance, and 25% are chosen randomly. Additionally, the focus is on whether products are intended for professional or private use, with a priority given to products for professional use. The PPPs analysed in 2023 were selected on the basis of the following criteria: all the products contained active substances included in the price list agreed with the laboratory, were approved for professional use in Sweden and were in distributors' stocks. Most of the products had been included in previous programmes due to high sales volumes, and a few of them were among the products that the Nordic countries had agreed to analyse. While products with previous non-compliance issues were considered, they could not be included in the plan.
The tasks related to the authorisation and control on the marketing and use of PPPs have not been delegated and are carried out by the CAs. Conclusions on delegation of certain tasks

recommendations.text: To ensure the reliability and relevance of PPP analyses, and in particular that: · Samples of PPPs are analysed to determine the presence of unacceptable co-formulants set out in Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 and the content of impurities whose maximum content is established in the approval of relevant active substances, as referred to Article 6(b) of the same Regulation. This is to comply with Article 24(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. · Sampling is carried out in line with Articles 2(1) 34(5) and 35 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Recommendation is based upon conclusions Nos 55 and 62

citations.text: This approach does not comply with Articles 2(1), 14(h) 24(1) and 34(5) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, as samples collected and sent by the operators cannot be considered as part of official controls. It is also not correct to allow for a counter sample without meeting all the conditions outlined in Article 35 of the same regulation.

The laboratory reports of the samples analysed in recent years revealed only a few non- compliant results. Apart from a reservation on the independence of the sampling, referred to above, it would provide reasonable assurance that PPPs marketed are those that have 11 been authorised. From 2018 to 2023, analyses were conducted on 19, 50, 20, 19, 24, and 29 products respectively, with only three cases of non-compliance detected during this period.

The laboratory carrying out the analysis for the quality control of PPPs is designated and accredited to ISO/IEC 17025. However, not including analyses for unacceptable co- formulants and regulated impurities in the sampling programme reduces the overall capability of the control system to ensure the safety of the PPPs placed on the market.

recommendations.text: To ensure the quality, consistency and effectiveness of official controls, in particular that: · Information and checklists provided to inspectors cover the verification of all relevant aspects of compliance of operators with articles 28, 55, 65 and 67 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009. · There is supervision of the inspectors, to identify and correct any weaknesses in their performance. · Inspections are comprehensive and cover all premises and all relevant aspect of marketing and use of PPPs. This is to comply with Articles 4(2)(a), 5 (1)(a) and (b), 12(1) and 14(b)(i) (ii)(iv) and (e) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Recommendation is based upon conclusions Nos 32, 33, 79 and 93

citations.text: A Danish laboratory, accredited to ISO/IEC 17025, has been designated for performing tests to analyse the formulation quality of PPPs.

The audit team noted that the primary aim of inspections, both at market and user levels, is to verify basic compliance aspects without further thorough verification. This lack of verification had not been detected by CAs, as not all of them had carried out an audit at the time of this audit. This oversight deficiency does not comply with Articles 5(1) (a) and (b) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The CA indicated that a recent report identified these issues and acknowledged the need for better collaboration and supervision of activities carried out by the MUPs. Conclusions on the competent authorities for official controls
The roles and responsibilities of the CAs are clearly defined, with cooperation between CAs.
The audit team observed three inspections conducted by two MUPs at two retailers/distributors selling PPPs for professional use and at a garden centre selling PPPs for non-professional use.

The inspectors carried out an exhaustive check of the conditions of the storage with the aim to ensure that storage of PPPs is safe and that operators have all measures in place to avoid contamination of the surroundings in case of accident.

The audit team interviewed the customs officials at the border control post and noted that the officials were well-versed in the procedures and authorised to sign import approvals. According to the procedure, Customs carries out controls at the import points of any consignment of PPPs or active substances declared by importers and identified by relevant tariff codes. The SCA presented good examples of collaboration with customs to detect the illegal trade of PPPs. The audit team visited the custom offices and the custom warehouse where a physical check was carried out. The customs officials conduct documentary checks for all imports of PPPs and active substances notified, ensuring all documents in the import approval are reviewed. If there are any uncertainties, customs officials can contact the SCA for clarification.

The inspectors reviewed the application records to confirm that they contained the minimum information required by the checklist, but did not cross-check the accuracy and reliability of these records. They do not request invoices to verify whether PPPs recorded were purchased or if recorded quantities are realistic for use on the corresponding areas where PPPs were used. This lack of verification goes against Article 14(e) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and Article 55 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 and prevents a technical evaluation of PPP usage. 16

Inspections do not always include visits to areas where PPPs were used, even when crops are present. Inspectors indicated that their checklists do not prompt visits to areas where PPPs were used. Some inspectors reported they might visit a few areas where PPPs were used, while others do not, as it is not required. The lack of guidance in the inspection procedure is not in line with Article 12(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, and systematically omitting visits to areas where PPPs were used is not in line with Article 14(b)(i) and (d), limiting data collection and reducing the likelihood of detecting unauthorised PPP applications (missing of information about crops and areas cultivated, buffer zones, water courses, etc).

There are some IT programmes developed by the SBA that are very useful for the proper application of PPPs. The farmers visited used such programmes. Another positive aspect that the audit team noted during all their visits to farms, is that measures to limit or avoid the contamination of water courses or ground waters are always checked. Control of non-agricultural users

The audit team examined cases of non-compliances found during MUPs inspections and noted that the follow-up is satisfactory, and sanctions are imposed on the non-compliant operators, including the taking of corrective actions. Evidence of these was provided to the audit team. Conclusions on controls on the use of plant protection products
